name: Scalp micropigmentation

lead: Scalp micropigmentation (SMP), also called a hair tattoo, is a non-surgical cosmetic tattoo that gives a bald or thinning scalp the look of a close buzz cut or greater density. It also conceals hair transplant scars and burn or other scars on the head. The effect is immediate and camouflages rather than regrows hair.

Pigment is placed superficially in the epidermis and upper dermis to mimic tiny hair follicles, with color matched to the person's hair. In looksmaxxing forums it is compared with hair transplants and hair systems for men who prefer a buzzed look. Wikipedia's article cites news and magazine sources rather than clinical studies.

paras: Treatment typically takes three to four sessions of about two hours each. People usually keep the head cropped to match the pigment, and practitioners may patch-test for ink allergy.

Poor technique can produce an unnatural hairline. Wikipedia reports that the result is permanent but can be removed by laser, and notes that its statement about no scientific data on side effects lacks a citation.

angle.text: Scalp micropigmentation tattoos tiny pigment dots onto the scalp to look like a close buzz cut or denser hair, and to conceal transplant and other scalp scars. The visual effect is immediate; it camouflages rather than regrows hair.

lead: Scalp micropigmentation (SMP), also called a hair tattoo, is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which tiny dots of pigment are placed in the scalp to look like hair follicles [1]. People use it to get the look of a close-cropped haircut on a bald or thinning head, to make thin areas look denser, and to hide hair-transplant scars or scars from burns and injury [1][2][3].

Pigment is deposited more superficially than in a conventional tattoo, in the epidermis and upper dermis, and the shade is matched to the person's hair colour [1]. A course typically takes three to four sessions of about two hours each, with the hairline treated as the most important element of the design [1]. The effect is immediate, visual and cumulative across sessions, and it needs no daily upkeep beyond sun care and occasional touch-ups.

SMP does not grow hair; its effect is visual density. Clinical reviews describe it as a camouflage option alongside medication and hair transplantation, and a 2022 review calls it a major means of hair-loss treatment alongside them [4][2][5]. A 2021 case series reported high satisfaction and minimal fading [3]. In looksmaxxing forums it is weighed against hair transplants and hair systems, with some users favouring it for a shaved look and others preferring other options [6].
infobox: Three to four sessions of about two hours [1]
Described as permanent; removable by laser [1]
Buzz-cut look, density for thinning, scar concealment [1][2]

paras: Practitioners use cosmetic tattoo instruments and pigments in a stippling pattern across the scalp, placing separate dots that resemble closely cut hair [2][7]. A 2013 review describes SMP as a medical tattoo process that must be customised for each patient because skin differs in how it holds pigment, calls it labour-intensive and says that up to about 20 hours of procedure time may be needed in some cases [8].

Trichoscopy of treated skin shows evenly spaced, round, grey-to-black dots that look somewhat larger than the neighbouring follicles, and a 2022 case report correlated this appearance with histology [7]. A 2022 review aimed at doctors covers the procedures, the most frequent patient complaints and practical tips for a natural result [4].

Men with pattern baldness use SMP to look as if they have a closely shaved head with an intact hairline, and people with diffuse thinning use it to reduce the contrast between hair and scalp [1][6]. Wikipedia's article says it is performed on all ethnicities and that the hairline is one of the most crucial parts of the treatment [1]. It is also used to conceal linear scars from strip hair-transplant surgery and other scalp scars [1][2].

Reviews present SMP for androgenetic alopecia, alopecia areata, scarring (cicatricial) alopecias, chemotherapy-related hair loss and transplant deformities [4][2][5]. A dermatotrichology review lists it among the more permanent camouflage options, in a range that starts with hairpieces, wigs and toupees [5].
Microblading, a related cosmetic-tattoo technique, has been used to address the look of thinning at hairlines [1].

Hair-restoration reviews present camouflage as one tool in a combined approach with medication, hair transplantation and adjuncts, and a 2021 review discusses combination approaches to hair loss in men, women and children [9][10]. A 2013 review notes that SMP can be used where transplant results are unsatisfactory [8]; the 2021 case series described it as an adjunct to transplantation in some men and a choice for people who decline transplantation [3].

Practitioners may perform a small patch test on an inconspicuous part of the scalp to check for ink allergy [1]. The ink colour is matched to the current hair colour, and treatment is spread across several sessions [1]. In the 2021 case series, patients had three weekly sessions plus a touch-up about one month after the last session [3]. The hairline can be adjusted or touched up over time [1].
Cost depends on location, clinic proximity and the extent of hair loss [1].

Wikipedia names a poorly executed hairline as the main risk, noting that such a hairline can look unnatural although it can be adjusted or touched up [1]. Allergic reactions to ink are the reason for patch testing [1]. In the 2021 series of 22 patients, one had an allergic reaction and no serious adverse effects were reported; fading was minimal over follow-up of 7 to 32 months [3].

The pigment is described as permanent but removable with laser treatment [1]. A 2015 review of the technique discusses the histology and physiology of tattoo pigments in skin and summarises how tattooing is regulated by the FDA and US states [2].

On looksmax.org, SMP is discussed as a shaved-head option and compared with hair systems and transplants [6]. One user says it suits those who always wear a bald look, those with gaps after a poor FUE transplant and those with diffuse thinning, and that it does little for typical male pattern baldness, naming hair systems as the better route; another adds that having a skull shape suited to a buzz cut is a key condition [6]. Users in the same thread admire a member's hair system as a bigger 'looksmax' than his jaw [6].
Published work consists mainly of narrative reviews, technique descriptions and small series rather than controlled trials.

A 2013 review by Rassman, Pak and Kim described SMP as a labour-intensive medical tattoo process needing customisation [8]. A 2015 review by Rassman, Pak, Kim and Estrin presented the technique for alopecias refractory to treatment and for hair-transplant deformities, reporting very high patient satisfaction and calling SMP a good nonsurgical alternative that its authors expected to become a standard offering for cosmetic office practices [2]. A 2021 craniofacial surgery case series (Seyhan and Kapi) followed 22 patients treated between 2017 and 2020: 16 men and 6 women, with male or female pattern hair loss, alopecia areata or scalp scars. Follow-up averaged 20 months, 80% of patients (all the women) were very satisfied and all would recommend it [3].

A 2024 retrospective study of 40 women with female pattern hair loss, 23 of whom had hair transplantation and 17 SMP, used Folliscope measurements and ROC analysis; the authors found hair density the most important factor in choosing between the procedures and suggested SMP for densities of at least 104.6 hairs per square centimetre [11]. A 2022 case report characterised SMP dots by trichoscopy and histology [7]. A 2022 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology called SMP a widely used technique to camouflage scalp scars and alopecia [4].

claims.claim: SMP suits mainly men who always wear a bald look, have gaps from a poor FUE, or have diffuse thinning.
Skull shape matters for pulling off the buzzed look.
Hair systems are superior to SMP.
SMP is permanent and fades little.
A bad SMP hairline can look unnatural.
SMP can be a choice for women with female pattern hair loss as well as men.

timeline.event: Rassman, Pak and Kim publish a review describing SMP as a medical tattoo process for balding or thinning hair. [8]
A Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology review presents SMP as a concealer for hair and scalp deformities and covers tattoo regulation. [2]
Patients in a later craniofacial case series receive SMP. [3]
A craniofacial surgery case series of 22 patients reports high satisfaction and minimal fading; a review covers combination approaches to hair loss. [3][10]
Reviews on natural-looking SMP results and on hair camouflage are published, and a case report links SMP trichoscopy to histology. [4][5][7]
A retrospective study compares hair transplantation and SMP in women with female pattern hair loss. [11]
